analysis.one_liner: Let the President waive environmental and permitting laws to fast-track oil shale and tar sands drilling on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in either committee it was referred to, and died when Congress adjourned in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the President to waive whatever laws he judged necessary to speed up oil shale and tar sands production on federal land, with no requirement to follow normal agency procedures. Court challenges would have been restricted to constitutional claims filed within 60 days, with appeals going only to the Supreme Court. Half of the federal royalties from the new production would have gone to private research grants on carbon capture, alternative fuels, and energy efficiency. The bill was never acted on by either committee it was sent to and died at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies interested in developing the oil shale and tar sands deposits on federal land would have gained the most: a President empowered to waive whatever environmental, permitting, or procedural laws slowed them down, and a legal system where only constitutional claims filed within 60 days could even be heard. Recipients of the royalty-funded private research grants would also have gained a new revenue stream.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas developers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: It ordered the President to limit the application of existing laws — including the permitting process — as needed to speed up exploration and production of oil and gas from oil shale and tar sands on federal lands.

It explicitly freed the President from the Administrative Procedure Act's rulemaking requirements when acting under the bill, removing the usual public-comment and explanation steps for agency decisions.
It restricted court challenges to constitutional claims filed within 60 days, appealable only to the Supreme Court, making it much harder to contest development decisions.
It dedicated half of federal royalties from the new production to private grants for carbon-capture research, alternative fuels, and energy efficiency.

analysis.who_pays: The public would have paid twice. First, the usual environmental review and public-comment safeguards that apply to drilling on federal land would have been suspended at the President's discretion. Second, half of the royalties the government collects for extracting publicly owned resources would have been diverted to private grants, shrinking the money returning to the Treasury. Citizens also would have lost most legal recourse, since non-constitutional claims were barred outright.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weakened safeguards and lost royalties

drawbacks.text: The bill let the President waive, at his sole discretion, whatever laws he decided were necessary to speed oil shale and tar sands production, and it exempted his actions from the federal Administrative Procedure Act — the law requiring agencies to follow open procedures and explain their decisions.

It sharply limited public recourse: lawsuits could only allege constitutional violations, had to be filed within 60 days, and could be appealed only by petitioning the Supreme Court, with no lower appellate review.
Half of the royalties the federal government collected from production would be diverted into private grants rather than returned to the Treasury, reducing revenue from resources owned by the public.
Oil shale and tar sands fuels are carbon-intensive, and the bill's response to that was a royalty-funded research program rather than any requirement to limit emissions from the production itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered one clear public benefit: faster development of domestic oil shale and tar sands as a response to 2008 energy prices. But it bought that speed by handing the President sole discretion to suspend any law standing in the way of production, cutting the public out of the environmental review and comment process, and sharply limiting citizens' ability to sue [S3]. Diverting half of federal royalties into private grants removed money the Treasury would otherwise collect [S2]. Even setting aside the environmental stakes, the design — one-person waiver authority with almost no judicial check — gave away public lands protections with no meaningful accountability, a cost that clearly outweighed the speed it promised.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in June 2008, never got a hearing or a floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Cannon introduced the bill on June 9, 2008, and it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and the House Science and Technology Committee.
Eleven days after introduction it was further referred to subcommittees — Energy and Mineral Resources and Energy and Environment — where it remained without any hearings, markups, or votes.
On September 11, 2008, Cannon filed a discharge petition, a procedure meant to force a bill out of committee onto the floor; the petition did not succeed.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's environmental and legal protections on federal lands stayed intact. Oil shale developers remained subject to the normal permitting and review process instead of the bill's blanket waivers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; existing environmental protections stayed intact

Companies would get faster access to public resources with fewer conditions attached.

industries.note: Half the federal royalties from new production would flow to private grants for carbon capture, alternative fuels, and efficiency research — a subsidy funded by cutting the Treasury's take in half.

The public owns the oil shale and tar sands on federal lands. The bill would have diverted half the royalties owed to the government into private grants, and expedited extraction of those resources with reduced environmental review.
